paras: The lynching of Ransom O'Neal and Charles Tunstall was the shooting of two Black prisoners in their cell in the county jail at Angleton, Texas, late on the night of January 13, 1903, by several unnamed men. The two were awaiting trial on a charge of murdering County Attorney Ed C. Smith, and several white headlines presented the killers as his avengers. The Associated Press dispatch ran across the country, and in the Black press the St. Paul Appeal condemned the killing as "outrageous butchery."

In its review of the past year's Texas events, the Houston Daily Post recorded that County Attorney Ed C. Smith of Brazoria county had been "killed and Deputy Sheriff Cochran Willis wounded by negroes at Columbia." According to the wire, O'Neal and Tunstall were charged with Smith's murder at Columbia "several weeks ago" and were held in the county jail at Angleton with a number of other Black prisoners. None of the reports describes their arrest or the evidence against them.

A dispatch dated Angleton, January 14, said that "late last night" several men entered the cell where the two were confined and shot them to death. Before firing, the men warned the other prisoners to cover their heads with blankets, which they did. The bedding on the cots of the two men then caught fire, and O'Neal had an arm and a leg burned off; the reports do not say how the fire started.
The attackers were not named, and the dispatch gave no number beyond "several men." No jailer, sheriff or guard is mentioned in any account of the night.

No report of an inquest, an arrest, or a grand jury inquiry into the killings appears in the coverage. The deaths were later entered in Black papers' annual lynching lists: the Seattle Republican listed both men as "colored, Angleton, Tex.," under January 14, and the Sedalia Times and the Chicago Broad Ax listed them under the same date with the charge of murder.

The Associated Press account appeared on January 15 and 16 in papers from Montana to Georgia, nearly word for word but under very different headlines. Several papers told the story from the attackers' side: the St. Louis Republic headed it "Citizens Avenge the Murder of Attorney Ed C. Smith," the Washington Times "Jail Broken Into by Avengers of Murdered County Attorney," and the Savannah Morning News "NEGRO MURDERERS KILLED IN JAIL." The Omaha Daily Bee wrote of a mob executing "Summary Vengeance on Alleged Texan Murderers," keeping the guilt of the dead men in doubt.

Other papers used plainer terms: the Montgomery Advertiser's headline read "LYNCHED IN THEIR CELL," the Arizona Republican's "A SLAUGHTER IN JAIL," and the Butte Inter Mountain's "MOB SHOOTS." Weeklies carried the story to the end of January, with the River Falls Journal in Wisconsin attributing the killing to "a Posse of Men" and the Fair Play of Ste. Genevieve, Missouri, reprinting the wire on January 24.

Black papers first carried the same dispatch: the Cleveland Gazette ran a shortened version on January 17 as "Were Shot to Death by a Mob," and the State Ledger printed it as a "Special" on January 20. The St. Paul Appeal quoted the dispatch in a January 17 editorial, rendering "negroes" as "Afro-Americans," and asked whether the killing was not "a wanton, unpardonable, unjustifiable, outrageous butchery." The Appeal allowed that the men "may have been guilty" but argued that they were in jail awaiting trial and, as citizens born in the United States, were entitled to the rights of any other citizen. It went on to protest against "white men taking the law in their own hands" and warned that such a state of affairs "cannot much longer continue."

Reports differ on the night of the attack. The first dispatches, dated January 14, said "late last night," and later copies said "late Tuesday night," both pointing to January 13. The State Ledger's version said "Thursday night" and the Manning Times said "Wednesday night," while the year-end lists gave January 14, the date of the first dispatch. The names also vary from copy to copy, with O'Neal appearing as O'Neil, O'Neill, Oneal and "Ramson," and Tunstall as "Tunestall."

reader.title: Lynching of Ransom O'Neal and Charles Tunstall
bases: Several men entered a county jail cell and shot two Black prisoners held on a murder charge to death (A3, A5, A12).

Two prisoners awaiting trial were shot to death in their cell by 'several men', a 'mob' in headlines, with no lawful authority (A3, A5, A13); headlines presented the killing as vengeance for the murder of the county attorney they were charged with (A3, A6).

Every contemporary report, white and Black, reprints or rewrites one Angleton wire dispatch (A2, A3, A12, A16); later year-end lynching lists (A20, A21, A22) repeat the event but add no independent account, and no local Texas report was found.

accounts.label: Wire report (Angleton dispatch)
accounts.gist: Several men entered the jail cell late at night, had the other prisoners cover their heads, and shot O'Neal and Tunstall to death; bedding caught fire and O'Neal lost an arm and a leg to burns; the two were charged with murdering County Attorney Smith.

accounts.label: Black editorial (St. Paul Appeal)
accounts.gist: Quoting the dispatch, the Appeal called the killing 'outrageous butchery' and argued that the men, whatever their guilt, were citizens awaiting trial and entitled to their constitutional rights.

accounts.label: Year-end lynching lists
accounts.gist: Lists both men as lynched at Angleton, Tex., on January 14, 1903, for murder.

framing.detail: The St. Louis Republic headed the wire 'Citizens Avenge the Murder of Attorney Ed C. Smith' and the Washington Times 'Jail Broken Into by Avengers of Murdered County Attorney'.
The Savannah Morning News called the victims 'NEGRO MURDERERS' and the Omaha Daily Bee wrote of 'Summary Vengeance on Alleged Texan Murderers'.

The Montgomery Advertiser ('LYNCHED IN THEIR CELL'), Arizona Republican ('A SLAUGHTER IN JAIL'), Butte Inter Mountain ('MOB SHOOTS') and River Falls Journal ('by a Posse of Men') ran the wire without comment.
The Cleveland Gazette ran the wire as 'Were Shot to Death by a Mob' and the State Ledger as 'Two Negroes Shot to Death'.
The St. Paul Appeal's editorial called it 'a wanton, unpardonable, unjustifiable, outrageous butchery' and protested white men 'taking the law in their own hands'.

versions.value: 'Late last night' in dispatches dated Jan. 14, i.e. the night of Jan. 13

conflicts.note: The earliest dispatches, dated Jan. 14, say 'last night', which agrees with 'Tuesday night' (Jan. 13); the Wednesday and Thursday versions appear only in later rewrites, and the lists' Jan. 14 matches the dispatch date.
Spelling variants of two names in copies of one dispatch; Ransom O'Neal and Charles Tunstall are the most common forms.

record_check.dossier: Supported: night of Tuesday, Jan. 13 ('late last night' in Jan. 14 dispatches); year lists give Jan. 14, two rewrites say Wednesday or Thursday night.

record_check.record: Charles Tunstall, Ransom O'Neal, Ramson Oneal, Ransom O'Neill
record_check.dossier: Two victims only: Ransom O'Neal and Charles Tunstall; 'Ramson Oneal' and 'Ransom O'Neill' are spellings of O'Neal, not further victims.
0 separately injured: the burns were to O'Neal, who is counted among the two killed; no other prisoner is reported hurt.
Unnamed 'several men'; called a 'mob', 'Citizens', 'Avengers' or 'a Posse of Men' in headlines.
